1. Project Overview¶

This notebook demonstrates an end-to-end approach to financial fraud detection using a combo of advanced feature engineering, machine learning, and synthetic data generation using neural networks (GANs). The analysis is designed to reflect real world fraud data and how to predict 1st or 3rd party fraud.

Data Sources¶

The primary data for this project comes from the PaySim Synthetic Mobile Money Transactions Dataset, which contains one month of real-world mobile money transactions. PaySim’s logs include over 6 million records, with a variety of transaction types, customer behaviors, and injected fraudulent activity.

Augmenting the Data with GANs¶

In addition to the original Kaggle data, this project demonstrates synthetic data generation using Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs). To further enrich the dataset, I generated additional synthetic data using a GANs, specifically CTGAN. GANs are powerful machine learning models that can learn the underlying distribution of a dataset and generate new, highly realistic records. They are a family of deep learning models that can learn the statistical properties of a real dataset and create entirely new, artificial records identical to real data (and you can always add rules/restrictions etc based on business needs).

  • GANs allow us to create much larger and more varied datasets that are especially useful in rare event scenarios like fraud where we usually have a huge class imbalance, meaning way more non-fraud recaords vs. fraud for our models to learn from. This can be mediated using the class weighting parameters in any ML model but in my experience working with fraud data for various clients, I have found that augumentaion the dataset genereally improves model performance.
  • We can inject or simulate new types of risk patterns and attributes, such as device, geo, behavioral, and flag-based features etc, as done for this project.

Final Dataset¶

In this notebook, GANs are used (via the CTGAN implementation) to create the augmented synthetic dataset, synthetic_fraud_200k.csv, containing 200,000 synthetic transaction records. The process adds additional attributes such as device type, location, VPN usage, and risk flags by engineering these features.

Data Ingestion and Synthetic Data Generation Steps¶

  • Ingesting the original PaySim CSV (after download from Kaggle)
  • Creating engineered features
  • Training a GAN (CTGAN) on a stratified sample
  • Generating and saving the synthetic dataset for modeling

2. Feature Engineering: Translating Domain Knowledge into Additional Features¶

  • After reviewing the data and main risk indicators, I create new features that capture fraud-related behavior, like account draining, risk flag counts, and device or location usage patterns.
  • This step includes one-hot encoding categorical variables, applying log transforms to skewed numeric fields, and handling missing values.
  • The goal is to give the models better information so the models can more effectively identify fraud patterns.

Engineering Fraud-Focused Features and Cleaning Data¶

  • This function creates new variables that capture fraud risk factors, ratio-based features, operational flags, and time-based patterns.
  • Log scaling helps control for outliers; ratios highlight unusual behavior, and counting risk flags help with identifying txns with multiple warnings sign.
  • One-hot encoding or normalize/stadardizing the data may not be needed for boosting algorithms since they can do that autmatically but are generally just easier to work with when modelling.
    • One-hot encoding is usually still needed for categorical variables (even for boosting trees, unless they natively support categorical handling, like in CatBoost, LightGBM) but is generally not needed for tree-based methods (like XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost), as they are not sensitive to feature scale, but it doesn’t hurt.
    • The main benefit of encoding/scaling is “consistency” across different models, and sometimes for interpretability or pre-processing pipelines.
Shape after feature engineering: (200000, 49)

Insights:

  • The resulting dataframe now contains the following new features:

    • Amount ratios (amt_over_oldbal, amt_over_destbal): If transactions are unusually high compared to the available balance, these features can help spot draining, laundering, or suspicious fund movement.

    • Balance change features (org_balance_delta, dest_balance_delta): Useful for flagging rapid or unexpected changes in account balances, which are often warning signs of fraud.

    • Account draining indicators (drain_amount, drained_to_zero): Catches scenarios where an account is fully emptied in a single move, which could indicate account takeover (ATO).

    • High-amount and type-specific outlier flag: Highlights if a transaction is much larger than others, flagging it as a potential anomaly.

    • Time-based variables (hour, day_of_week, is_night, is_weekend): These may provide insight into when fraud is more likely to occur, such as during nights or weekends.

    • Risk stacking (risk_factor_count): Counts the number of separate risk signals to spot transactions with multiple suspicious indicators.

    • In real financial fraud data, there is usually an opportunity to create several more engineered features depending on what features the business has.

      • For example, if account balances, transaction amounts, etc., are provided, many more features can be created. Such features can be bucketed or used to create new interaction features.
      • This analysis does not get into interaction features, but in my real-world work, these are very useful to create and are quite important when modeling.
      • In essence, you should help the model understand underlying patterns as best as possible via engineered features created using interactions between existing features (like multiplying key numerical columns, ratios, boolean flags, cross features, etc.).
      • Before any modeling, it is good practice to run the features through a feature importance algorithm before and after modeling (using things like permutation importance or SHAP).

Visualizing Fraud Class¶

Distribution of Fraud vs. Non-Fraud Transactions

  • This plot shows that the synthetic dataset was created with a balanced number of fraudulent and non-fraudulent transactions.
  • A balanced class distribution like this is useful for model development and benchmarking, as it removes the extreme class imbalance that is common in real-world fraud data as mentioned earlier.
Plot 2: Fraud vs. Non-Fraud after sample and GANs

Visualizing Top 15 Features with Greatest Difference in Class (fraud vs non fraud)¶

Plot 3: Fraud vs. All Categorical

Plot 3: Fraud vs. All Categorical

Plot 3: Fraud vs. All Categorical

Plot 3: Fraud vs. All Categorical

Plot 3: Fraud vs. All Categorical

Insights:

  • Most non-fraud transactions have zero risk factors. Fraud cases are much more likely to have two or more stacked risk flags.
  • Fraud is concentrated in CASH_OUT and TRANSFER transaction types. Legit transactions are mainly found in PAYMENT and CASH_IN.
  • Tor browser and VPN use are rare for non fraud but common for fraud.Fraudsters usually do rely heavily on these IP anonymizing tools, so that makes sense to see here.
  • High-amount transactions are much more likely to be fraud.
  • Behavioral flags like multi_account, new_account, and night_txn are more frequent in fraud. These patterns should help our model pick up fraudulent tactics.
  • Fraud transactions more often involve clicking suspicious email links. This adds another layer of behavioral evidence that makes sense logically and should help our model in identifying fraud.
  • Device and location matter. Fraud is more likely on desktop and less likely in the loc_OTHER category.
  • Manual review and risk stacking features both point to higher fraud likelihood, giving clear signals for risk teams.
  • Fraud is also more common for accounts flagged as new. This tells us that fraudsters may be targeting recently opened accounts.


Time-Based Feature Distributions by Fraud Status¶

  • This code defines and uses a helper function to plot the distributions time based features created from the 'step' column we were provided, by the fraud label.
Plot 4: Fraud vs. Time based features

Plot 5: Fraud vs. Transaction count over hour of day

Insights:

  • The overall transaction volume stays almost totally flat for all hours of the day. This tells us that there’s no business-driven transaction surge at any specific time, so TOD (time-of-day) by itself doesn’t seem to separate fraud from non-fraud.
  • The fraud rate by hour is also extremely steady, with almost no difference between early morning, midday, or late night hours. Attackers may be distributing their activity to avoid time-based detection.
  • There’s a minimal variation in fraud rate across days of the week. No specific weekday or weekend effect is visible in this data; fraud risk remains consistent from Monday to Sunday.
  • The fraud rate doesn't change meaningfully between night and day transactions. Nighttime does not seem to pose any extra risk in this synthetic data.
  • There is also no significant difference in fraud risk between weekends and weekdays so these may not be the best predictors for our model.


Fraud Counts by Transaction Type¶

Plot 6: Fraud Counts by Transaction Type

Insights:

  • Fraud is heavily concentrated in CASH_OUT and TRANSFER transactions. These types account for the vast majority of fraud cases in the data.
  • Legitimate transactions make up the bulk of PAYMENT and CASH_IN activity, with very few fraud cases in these categories.
  • Both fraud and non-fraud counts are low for DEBIT, indicating this type is rare overall.
  • Transaction type clearly separates risky from safe activity, making it a key feature for our fraud model.


Exploring Risk Flags, Device, and Geo Patterns¶

  • This section focuses on risk signals such as VPN use, TOR browser (The Onion Router), suspicious IP, device type, and manual review triggers.
  • Fraud rates for each flag, highlighting which features actually separate fraud from normal activity and visualized below.
Plot 7: Fraud Counts by Fraud Rate by Device and Location and Other Similar Features

Insights:

  • Fraud is above 90% when multiple risk factors are stacked together, making risk_factor_count one of the strongest indicators in our data.
  • Tor browser and suspicious IP are very important since when either of these binary features is present (i.e has value of 1), the fraud rate reaches approx. 90% again.
  • Transactions with a suspicious zero destination after, or those flagged for manual review, show much higher fraud rates, typically around 50% or more.
  • VPN use and multi-account activity are both strong risk signals, with fraud nearly double when these are detected.
  • Two-factor authentication shows good indiciative value. Its associated with a lower fraud rate.


Investigating Correlations Among Features¶

  • This correlation heatmap compares the relationships between the top 25 categorical and binary features and the fraud target using Cramer’s V, a correlation measure which is suited for categorical vars.
  • Cramer’s V is used here because it handles binary and multi-class features, and finds non-linear associations that might be missed by linear methods.
  • The upper triangle heatmap displays all pairwise correlations, with red boxes marking feature pairs that are significantly related.
Plot 8: Cramer's V Correlation Heatmap

Insights:

  • Risk factor count has strong overlap with key risk flags like browser_tor and suspicious_ip, which makes sense since it aggregates these indicators.
  • Several fraud flags, including suspicious_ip, browser_tor, vpn_used, and type_TRANSFER, often appear together in the same transactions.
  • Transaction type and device features show much weaker correlation, meaning they add fresh signals that aren’t just repeats of other risk flags.
  • No signs of direct leakage but the stacked risk feature, 'risk factor count' is highly related and could be a cuase of collinearity in the model.

4. Hyperparameter Tuning and Model Training¶

  • We will be training 3 models to compare performnace and be thorough.
  • With the new features engineered, the next step will be to tune each model’s key parameters to get the best possible fraud detection performance.
  • Grid search and cross-validation are used to find the optimal hyperparameters.
  • Hyperparameter tuning will be done before final training and testing, which keeps evaluation realistic and ensures all models are compared fairly.
  • Three models are trained and evaluated: Logistic Regression for a baseline, plus Random Forest and LightGBM as our main prediction models. Performance is measured using AUC/ROC and precision-recall metrics.
  • Depending on the client, they may be more interested in simply minimizing false positives or reducing false negatives, depending on their incurred costs when losing a potential customer or when allowing a fraudster through.

Hyperparameter Tuning with Grid Search¶

  • Splitting the dataset into training and testing partitions, using stratification to maintain the same fraud rate in both sets.
  • This code below runs grid search over multiple combinations of tree depth, number of trees, and other model settings for both Random Forest and LightGBM. The best hyperparameters are then selected for final model evaluation.
  • The code will also save the best hyperparameters into a local drive to avoid rerunning the code and maintaining consistent models.

Insights:

  • Increasing tree depth and the number of estimators improves performance up to a limit.
  • LightGBM works best with a lower learning rate to balance accuracy and overfitting.
  • Tuning these settings before training gives a better shot at catching rare fraud than just using the defaults.

Model Training and Evaluation with Multiple Metrics¶

  • Each model is trained and tested using a full set of evaluation metrics, including ROC AUC, precision-recall AUC, and the confusion matrix.
  • ROC and precision-recall curves help show how well the model separates fraud from non-fraud, even when the data is imbalanced.
  • The confusion matrix summarizes the true positives, false positives, showing exactly where the model succeeds and where it struggles.

Fianl Model Insights¶

  • Model Performance Insights Tree-based models (Random Forest, LightGBM) outperform logistic regression on all metrics: ROC AUC, precision, recall, and F1 score.

  • LightGBM gives the best overall performance:

    1. Precision: 0.87
    2. Recall: 0.85
    3. F1: 0.86
    4. ROC AUC: 0.94
    5. PR AUC: 0.94

  • Logistic regression lags behind with a lower recall (0.70) and precision (0.69). This means it misses more frauds and generates more false positives than the tree-based models.

  • False positives and false negatives drop significantly with Random Forest and LightGBM. LightGBM catches more fraud with fewer mistakes:

    • LightGBM: 2,628 false positives, 3,104 false negatives

    • Random Forest: 2,746 FP, 3,172 FN

    • Logistic Regression: 6,182 FP, 6,014 FN

  • ROC and precision-recall curves for both tree models show strong separation between fraud and non-fraud, even with class imbalance. Both models maintain high precision across all recall levels, showing that our model flagged the fraud well.

  • Confusion matrices confirm the trend: tree-based models catch a high number of fraud cases while keeping false alarms low.

  • F1 scores close to 0.85 for both tree models signal a great ratio between catching fraud and limiting false alarms.

📖 5. Model Explainability¶

  • SHAP values are used here to show which features have the biggest impact on LightGBM’s predictions. This helps clarify what the model focuses on overall and also how it makes decisions on specific transactions..

SHAP Bubble Chart (Mean |SHAP| Impact per Feature)¶

This plot shows the average absolute impact of each feature across the whole test set.

The bubble size tells us how much, on average, that a feature moves the model’s prediction (regardless of direction, positive or negative).

It shows us which features are most important for the model.

Plot 11:SHAP Bubble Chart for Model Feature Performance

Insights:

  • browser_tor and risk_factor_count seem to be the top features, meaning that overall they are most influential in pushing the model towards predicting fraud or not fraud.
  • Features like step, suspicious_ip, and night_txn also show strong mean impact, signaling they consistently influence the prediction outcome.
  • The bubble sizes make it easy to compare overall importance and the colour gradient adds context about each feature’s typical value across the test set.
  • This plot helps spot the highest value features and gives us an idea for future feature selection when remodeling.

SHAP Beeswarm Plot:¶

  • This plot shows the individual transaction in our test set. Dots are spread out horizontally by their SHAP value (how much the feature pushed that specific prediction higher or lower for fraud).
  • It tells us how much each feature is influencing the model in different directions (positive/negative).
Plot 12:SHAP Beeswarm Chart for Top Feature Contributions

Insights:

  • Features like risk_factor_count and night_txn show not just high average importance, but also strong directionality and higher values almost always increase the model’s fraud prediction. Other features seem more nuanced and have mixed effects on the model.

6. What This Project Achieved¶

  • This notebook delivers an end-to-end pipeline for fraud detection using a mix of real-world and synthetic data.
  • Our exploratory analysis found out key risk drivers. Categorical, flag, and behavioral features like browser_tor, suspicious_ip, and risk_factor_count stood out as strong predictors, and visualizations made class imbalance, feature drift, and risk patterns very clear.
  • Custom feature engineering was performed, adding time-based signals, risk stacking, and ratio-based features. This made our dataset more realistic.
  • Visual reporting and summary tables were then outputted to easily interpret/compare model performances across all the metrics we chose to focus on. The most impactful features, best model settings, and confusion matrix results were included.
  • LightGBM achieved the strongest overall results:
    • Precision: 0.87 | Recall: 0.85
    • Lowest false positives (2,628) and false negatives (3,104) among all models.
  • Both LightGBM and Random Forest outperformed Logistic Regression by a wide margin on all key metrics, confirming that tree-based methods are much better suited to this fraud detection task.
